title: Comprehensive Neuro Set 1: Audition and Vestibular (Short Answer)

questions.prompt: Distinguish between sound "frequency" and "intensity" in terms of the units used to measure them.
questions.modelAnswer: Frequency is measured in Hertz (Hz); Intensity is measured in decibels (dB).

questions.prompt: What is the primary physiological purpose of the "impedance matching" performed by the middle ear ossicles?
questions.modelAnswer: To convert sound waves traveling through air (low acoustic impedance) into pressure waves in fluid (high acoustic impedance) without significant loss of energy.

questions.prompt: By what two mechanical mechanisms does the middle ear amplify sound pressure before it reaches the oval window?
questions.modelAnswer: The lever action of the ossicles and the ratio of the large surface area of the tympanic membrane to the small surface area of the oval window.

questions.prompt: In the cochlea, which specific chambers contain perilymph, and which one contains endolymph?
questions.modelAnswer: Scala vestibuli and scala tympani contain perilymph; scala media contains endolymph.

questions.prompt: How does the ionic composition of endolymph differ from standard extracellular fluid, and which structure is responsible for its secretion?
questions.modelAnswer: Endolymph has a high K^+and low Na^+concentration (similar to intracellular fluid); it is secreted by the stria vascularis.

questions.prompt: Explain the unique electrical driving force that causes K^+  to flow into auditory hair cells during depolarization.
questions.modelAnswer: The endolymph is positively charged (+80 mV) relative to the hair cell interior; this electrical gradient drives K^+into the cell even though the concentration gradient is minimal.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the roles of "inner hair cells" and "outer hair cells" in the process of auditory transduction.
questions.modelAnswer: Inner hair cells are the primary sensory transducers; outer hair cells exhibit "electromotility" (shortening/lengthening) to amplify the sensitivity of the inner hair cells.

questions.prompt: Define the "cochlear microphonic potential".
questions.modelAnswer: The oscillating receptor potential of the hair cells that faithfully reproduces the frequency of the sound stimulus.

questions.prompt: Describe the structural differences between the base and the apex of the basilar membrane that allow for frequency discrimination.
questions.modelAnswer: The base is narrow and stiff; the apex is wide and compliant.

questions.prompt: Which part of the basilar membrane (base or apex) is activated by high-frequency sounds?
questions.modelAnswer: The base (near the oval window).

questions.prompt: What is the neurotransmitter released by auditory hair cells onto the afferent fibers of the vestibulocochlear nerve?
questions.modelAnswer: Glutamate.

questions.prompt: Why do unilateral lesions of the central auditory pathways (distal to the cochlea) typically not result in total deafness in one ear?
questions.modelAnswer: Because auditory information is distributed bilaterally; some fibers cross the midline (lateral lemniscus) while others remain ipsilateral.

questions.prompt: What is the "tonotopic map" in the context of the auditory system?
questions.modelAnswer: The spatial mapping of sound frequencies along the basilar membrane, which is preserved throughout the auditory pathways to the cortex.

questions.prompt: Which specific structures of the vestibular organ are responsible for detecting angular (rotational) acceleration?
questions.modelAnswer: Semicircular canals.

questions.prompt: Which structures of the vestibular organ detect linear acceleration and the position of the head relative to gravity?
questions.modelAnswer: Otolith organs (utricle and saccule).

questions.prompt: Define the "kinocilium" and "stereocilia" in a vestibular hair cell.
questions.modelAnswer: The kinocilium is a single large cilium; stereocilia are a cluster of smaller cilia.

questions.prompt: Does bending the stereocilia toward or away from the kinocilium result in depolarization of the vestibular hair cell?
questions.modelAnswer: Toward the kinocilium (increases K^+conductance).

questions.prompt: What is the "cupula," and what is its role in the detection of head rotation?
questions.modelAnswer: A gelatinous mass in the ampulla that covers the hair cells; it is displaced by endolymph flow during rotation, bending the cilia.

questions.prompt: Contrast the specific planes of movement detected by the utricle versus the saccule.
questions.modelAnswer: Utricle detects horizontal acceleration/head tilt; Saccule detects vertical acceleration (e.g., an elevator).

questions.prompt: What are "otoliths" (statoconia), and where are they found?
questions.modelAnswer: Calcium carbonate crystals; they are found in the maculae of the utricle and saccule.

questions.prompt: Define "nystagmus" and explain how the direction of the nystagmus is defined (by the fast or slow component).
questions.modelAnswer: An involuntary eye movement with a slow and fast component; it is defined by the direction of the fast (rapid) component.

questions.prompt: During head rotation to the left, in which direction do the eyes initially move (slow component), and in which direction is the resulting nystagmus?
questions.modelAnswer: Eyes initially move right (slowly); the nystagmus is to the left (fast).

questions.prompt: What is "postrotatory nystagmus," and what is its direction relative to the original rotation?
questions.modelAnswer: Eye movement occurring after rotation stops; it is in the opposite direction of the original rotation.

questions.prompt: In the "caloric test," what direction of nystagmus is expected when warm water is used to rinse the ear?
questions.modelAnswer: Toward the treated side.

questions.prompt: Which brain stem structure is responsible for coordinating the "vestibulo-ocular reflex" to maintain a stable visual image during head movement?
questions.modelAnswer: Medial longitudinal fasciculus.
